Cultured populations of Caenorhabditis elegans maintained at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C] display highly stereotyped developmental timing. Embryogenesis proceeds rapidly, with the first L1 larva emerging from the egg after approximately half a day. This incubation period, termed the age at birth, is measured at 0.46 days [ab = 0.46 days] under these standard thermal conditions at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The newly hatched, free-swimming L1 larva is remarkably small, possessing a total length at birth of just 0.025 cm [Lb = 0.025 cm]. This minuscule size is accompanied by a correspondingly low wet weight at birth of 0.024 micrograms [Wwb = 0.024 micrograms]. These initial measurements underscore the extreme disparity between the neonatal and adult states in this species, which undergoes a four-fold increase in length and a nearly two-hundred-fold increase in mass over its lifetime.

The post-embryonic development of Caenorhabditis elegans proceeds through four larval stages, culminating in the molts to the L4 larva and finally to the reproductively active adult. The precise timing of these transitions is tightly coupled to the ambient temperature, with standard laboratory assays conducted at 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Under these conditions, the time since birth at puberty, defined as the interval from hatching to the final molt that yields a sexually mature individual, is typically 2.71 days since birth [tp = 2.71 days since birth] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. At this developmental landmark, the total length at puberty is routinely measured at 0.106 cm [Lp = 0.106 cm]. Concurrently, the wet weight at puberty reaches an average of 1.8 micrograms [Wwp = 1.8 micrograms], indicating substantial biomass accumulation during the pre-reproductive growth phase.

Once sexual maturation is complete, the reproductively active adult nematode enters a period of maximal fecundity. Under ideal conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is exceptionally high. Field and laboratory observations indicate that a single hermaphrodite can produce around 218 offspring per day [Ri = around 218 offspring per day] at the peak of its egg-laying activity. This prolific output is sustained for several days, contributing to a very high lifetime fecundity. The species continues to grow and increase in body mass after reaching reproductive maturity, a pattern common in many invertebrates. The ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum adult body mass, averages 4.3 micrograms [Wwi = 4.3 micrograms], more than double the mass recorded at the onset of puberty.

Growth in length also continues into the adult phase, though at a decelerating rate compared to the larval stages. The ultimate total length, or the maximum size attained by a fully grown adult, reaches approximately 0.14 cm [Li = approximately 0.14 cm]. This final size is only about thirty percent greater than the total length at puberty, illustrating that most axial elongation occurs during the pre-reproductive larval period. Under standard culture conditions at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the total lifespan, from the moment of hatching until natural death, is short. The maximum recorded longevity for Caenorhabditis elegans under these conditions is 21 days [am = 21 days], after which physiological senescence and mortality inevitably ensue at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].

The rapid pace of life in Caenorhabditis elegans, characterized by an age at birth of less than half a day (approximately 0.46 days) [ab = approximately 0.46 days] and a maximum lifespan of only 21 days [am = 21 days], exemplifies an opportunistically fast life history optimized for short-term resource pulses at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This strategy, which combines an extreme fecundity of hundreds of progeny per day with a remarkably compressed developmental timeline, contrasts sharply with the slower, more energy-conservative schedules observed in larger free-living nematodes such as those of the genus Plectus, where generation times often exceed two weeks even at comparable temperatures.
